title: Linear Jurisdictional Name Changes in Name Authority Records
summary: Only the latest name of a political jurisdiction whose territorial identity is essentially unchanged may be used as a subject heading or geographic subdivision (e.g. Sri Lanka, not Ceylon). Earlier names carry a 667 SUBJECT USAGE note in the name authority record stating they are not valid for subject use; validators should honor such notes. Mergers and splits are handled by H 710.
validation_rules: For a political jurisdiction that has had earlier names but whose territorial identity remains essentially unchanged, only the latest name is valid as a subject heading or as a geographic subdivision; earlier names are invalid in subject strings even though they are valid name headings (e.g. use `Sri Lanka`, not `Ceylon`). (H 708 Background)

If the name authority record for a geographic name has a 667 field beginning `SUBJECT USAGE:` stating the heading is not valid for use as a subject, reject that name as a subject heading or `$z` subdivision and use the later name named in the note. (H 708 Background, sec. 1)
Follow any instruction recorded in a 667 SUBJECT USAGE field of the authority record for the heading in question. (H 708 sec. 1)
For jurisdictional mergers and splits (territorial identity changed), apply H 710 instead. (H 708 sec. 3)

sections.heading: 1. Searching the name authority file
sections.text: When in doubt as to whether a given geographic name heading is valid for use as a subject heading, first search the LC Database to determine whether a decision has already been made and recorded in a 667 SUBJECT USAGE field. If this field is found in the authority record for the heading in question, follow the instructions as presented in the record.

sections.heading: 2. Adding usage decisions to name authority records
sections.text: Add a 667 SUBJECT USAGE field to new and existing geographic name headings for former names of political jurisdictions if the former name cannot be used as a subject heading because a later name is used.
